nature-res-177.title: Natural resource management: caring for land, water and life
nature-res-177.text: Strict preservation was supposed to save nature. In the 20th century people saw that it had not stopped resources declining, and a broader approach took in the social, economic and political sides. Natural resource management is the managing of land, water, soil, plants and animals with attention to how it affects life for people now and in the future. It deals with how people and natural landscapes interact, starting from the fact that livelihoods depend on healthy, productive land. It draws together heritage protection, land-use planning, water management, biodiversity conservation and the future of farming, mining, tourism, fishing and forestry. Its problems are complex and contested. Natural cycles are linked, so a change in one can have long-lasting, even irreversible, effects. Managers must also weigh many stakeholders, policies, politics, borders and economic effects. Mapping tools help. Geographic information systems, or GIS, overlay data sets such as rainfall, cleared land and erosion to plan where native bush should regrow.

nature-res-178.title: Who owns nature: four property regimes
nature-res-178.text: A lake fishery that anyone may use tends to be the most exploited of all. That observation sits at the center of a simple classification. Resource management approaches can be grouped by who holds rights over a resource: the state, a private owner, a group, no one, or a mix. Under state property, the state owns and controls the resource, and others use it only with permission, as in US national forests and parks. Under private property, a defined person or company owns the resource and bears both its benefits and its duties. Common property is in effect the private property of a group, such as a community forest. Open-access resources have no owner at all, and anyone may use them. Many real cases are hybrids. Native vegetation in New South Wales, for example, is protected in the public interest, but most of it grows on private land. These categories build on the wider study of {{ref:nature-econ-622}}.

nature-res-183.title: The commons: resources that belong to everyone
nature-res-183.text: Before 1968, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' were very rare. Then an article by {{ref:nature-hist-052}}, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', turned an old English legal term for common land into a general word for shared resources. The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth. The word can also mean resources a group of users governs for itself, through rules it creates, rather than through the state or the market. How a commons is run makes a large difference. In Mongolia, where herders moved together between pastures, grassland degradation was about 9%. Under state or household pastures it was about 75% in Russia and 33% in China. Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake in preventing overuse. Globalization brings new pressures. Fish and timber are sold on world markets, which makes their impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

nature-res-191.title: Enclosure: fencing off England's common land
nature-res-191.text: From the 1530s to the 1640s, enclosure riots were the leading form of social protest in England. Enclosure was the practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, stripping commoners of their traditional rights to use it. It merged scattered strips into large fields bounded by hedgerows, walls or fences, for the sole use of owners or their tenants. Parliament passed the first enclosure act in 1604. Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable. In Tudor England, high wool profits led lords to turn common fields into sheep pasture, evicting villagers. The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural workers moved to towns to become industrial workers. The Hammonds said it ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters. Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs. Many Marxists see it as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

nature-res-180.title: Community-based natural resource management
nature-res-180.text: People protect what is tied to their quality of life. That is one of the assumptions behind community-based natural resource management, which combines conservation goals with economic benefits for rural communities. It also assumes that locals are best placed to conserve resources, and that people conserve only when the benefits exceed the costs. It rests on subsidiarity, the principle of handling decisions at the most local level that can manage them. Social capital, the trust and networks within a community, and gender shape how it works in practice. It has critics. Tania Murray found that in upland Southeast Asia it could force communities to meet discriminatory conditions before gaining legal rights to resources.

nature-res-193.title: Community forestry: forests run by the people who live there
nature-res-193.text: In parts of Nepal, forest cover has risen by 37% under Forest User Groups run democratically by local people. That is community forestry, a participatory approach, prominent since the 1970s, in which local communities help manage forests and decide how land is used. The FAO defines it as any situation that closely involves local people in forestry. Communities manage forests for income from timber and {{ref:nature-res-174}}, and for services such as watershed protection and carbon storage. It is seen as one of the most promising ways to combine forest conservation with rural development and poverty reduction. Success depends on secure land tenure, which decides whether communities can invest in sustainable practices. Unclear boundaries, capture by local elites and weak enforcement threaten projects. Certification and carbon credits open global markets, but high certification costs remain a barrier for smallholders. There is no single blueprint, because regional conditions differ.

nature-res-187.title: The global commons: oceans, air and space
nature-res-187.text: Carbon dioxide that enters the atmosphere keeps driving climate change for at least a millennium. The atmosphere is part of the global commons, shared resource areas beyond the political reach of any single nation, along with the high seas, outer space and Antarctica. They hold {{ref:nature-econ-610}}s: goods that are costly but not impossible to keep users out of, and that are used up by use. So they suffer congestion, overuse and degradation, and their governance must avoid a worldwide {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. That is harder than locally. Global users are more varied, resources are less stable and harder to understand, and many are non-renewable on human time scales. Treaties between countries on the environment multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm conference. They are often slow, settle for the lowest common denominator and lack enforcement. There are successes. The {{ref:nature-clim-094}}, in force from 1 January 1989, is widely seen as a highly successful model. The 1961 Antarctic Treaty sets Antarctica aside as a scientific preserve with no military activity.

nature-res-184.title: Ostrom's design principles for a lasting commons
nature-res-184.text: Farmers in the Swiss Alps have run shared grazing land successfully for hundreds of years. Early work on the {{ref:nature-econ-606}} suggested every commons was doomed, but later economists found many that worked. {{ref:nature-hist-039}} won the Nobel Prize for analyzing them. From them she drew a set of design principles found in well-governed commons. They are clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognized rights to organize and nested enterprises. Graduated sanctions mean penalties that grow with repeated offenses. The principles work best when more than nine are used together. A related idea, the 'comedy of the commons', coined by Carol M. Rose in 1986, describes users policing themselves to keep or improve a commons.

nature-res-188.title: Common ownership: assets held as one
nature-res-188.text: Forms of common ownership exist in every economic system. Common ownership means holding an organization's or community's assets as one undivided whole, not in the names of individual members. Advocates separate collective ownership, shared by agreement among members such as a producer cooperative, from common property open to all, such as a public park. In capitalist economies it is practiced by voluntary associations, non-profits and, implicitly, all public bodies. Common ownership of the means of production is a central goal of socialist movements.

nature-res-190.title: Customary land: held by custom, not by title
nature-res-190.text: In Africa 90% of land is customary, and in Papua New Guinea 97%. Customary land is land held and used under unwritten local custom rather than written law. It is usually tied to indigenous communities, unlike statutory tenure, which was mostly brought in during colonial times. The gap between land the law recognizes and land managed by custom is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental damage. The World Bank and others promote formal land titles as a fix. Opinion is divided on whether this always helps the poor. Where several groups claim the same land, as often in Sub-Saharan Africa, formal titling can favor some and create tension.

nature-res-181.title: Integrated natural resource management
nature-res-181.text: Conflicts over resources are cheaper to prevent than to settle. Integrated natural resource management brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict. It manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic sides to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals. Sustainability is its focus. It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}.

nature-res-179.title: Stakeholder analysis: who has a stake in a forest
nature-res-179.text: Who has a stake in a river? The question sounds simple but is hard to answer, which is the main difficulty of stakeholder analysis. Borrowed from business management, it identifies the interest groups affected by how natural resources are used and conserved. Its stages include identifying decision-makers and stakeholders, investigating their interests, and mapping conflicts, trade-offs and synergies. One proposal would represent nature itself as a stakeholder. Many scholars have rejected it as hard to put into practice.

nature-res-199.title: Joint Forest Management in India
nature-res-199.text: In 1988 the Indian state of Odisha began an experiment in sharing its forests. Joint Forest Management is India's term for partnerships in which state forest departments and local communities share forest protection and development. It is set out in the National Forest Policy of 1988 and guidelines of 1990. Along with Nepal's Forest User Groups, it was an early response to failing centralized forest policy.

nature-res-185.title: Commoning: the commons as something people do
nature-res-185.text: A commons is not just a thing; it is also an activity. Commoning treats the commons as an ongoing practice, the process of people coming together to manage shared resources. Some authors separate three elements: the shared resources, the community that governs them, and commoning, the act of managing them together. In farming, commoning means looking after shared land jointly, and it matters to food systems in many communities worldwide.

nature-res-186.title: Urban commons: city spaces run by citizens
nature-res-186.text: A public square is not automatically a commons. The geographer David Harvey argued that public spaces become commons only when citizens take political action there. Urban commons are city resources managed by citizens themselves, valued by their use and upkeep costs rather than their market price. They work alongside the state and the market rather than replacing them.

nature-res-192.title: The open-field system before enclosure
nature-res-192.text: Before {{ref:nature-res-191}}, English common land lay under the lord of the manor. A manor was made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own farm, the demesne. Tenants held rights such as pasture, pannage, the right to let pigs forage, and estovers, the right to gather wood. Landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used. The system ended with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

nature-res-194.title: Ostrom's IAD framework for studying the commons
nature-res-194.text: Forests and pastures share a tricky pair of traits. They are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces what others get, and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical. To study how people manage such resources, {{ref:nature-hist-039}} built the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, or IAD. Built on {{ref:nature-econ-098}} assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, the positions of the people involved, called actors, and their formal and informal rules. It breaks complex problems of collective action into smaller 'action arenas'. Institutions are studied through seven types of rule: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

nature-res-189.title: Joint ownership and who controls an asset
nature-res-189.text: No contract can foresee everything. In the incomplete-contracts approach of Oliver Hart and colleagues, ownership matters for exactly that reason. The owner holds residual control rights, the say over an asset in any situation a contract does not cover. Owners have stronger incentives than non-owners to invest in a relationship, so ownership can ease the hold-up problem, where one party fears the other will exploit its investment. A central result is that joint ownership, where each party can veto use of the asset, is suboptimal. Later work shows it can be optimal when parties are unequally informed, in long-term relationships, or able to share know-how.

nature-res-195.title: The International Association for the Study of the Commons
nature-res-195.text: {{ref:nature-hist-039}} was a founding member and the first president of the International Association for the Study of the Commons. The non-profit was founded in 1989 to advance understanding of institutions for managing resources held or used in common. It publishes the open-access International Journal of the Commons and holds global conferences every two years.

nature-res-197.title: Governing the Commons: Ostrom's answer to Hardin
nature-res-197.text: Irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia: {{ref:nature-hist-039}} studied them all. The result was Governing the Commons (1990), her best-known book. It shows that communities worldwide have managed shared resources successfully through local rules. In it Ostrom set out eight design principles found in long-lasting institutions for managing shared resources. The book argues that self-interest need not cause degradation, contrary to the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. It can instead lead people to care for property they hold in common.

openers.managing-the-commons: Air, water and a habitable Earth belong to everyone, which raises an old question: who should look after them? Natural resource management is the work of caring for land, water, soil, plants and animals with an eye on people now and in the future. This chapter sorts resources by who holds the rights over them, the state, a private owner, a group or no one at all. It follows the commons from English common land, fenced off by enclosure, to community forests and the high seas beyond any nation's reach. Along the way it meets Elinor Ostrom, who found the rules that let shared resources thrive.

reviews.managing-the-commons: Who holds the rights to a resource shapes how it fares, and open-access resources that no one owns tend to be the most exploited. Hardin's 1968 article made the commons sound doomed, yet Ostrom found farmers in the Swiss Alps running grazing land for hundreds of years with clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions. Mongolia's shared pastures and Nepal's community forests showed the same pattern. England's enclosure moved the other way, turning common land into private fields and stripping commoners of their rights. At every scale, from customary land and urban commons to the atmosphere, the lesson is that rules made and enforced by users can keep a shared resource alive.
